newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi prince denies banks' link to "terrorism".
newsitem.headline: Saudi prince denies banks' link to "terrorism".

text.p: A Saudi prince, in remarks published on Thursday, denied unspecified allegations that Islamic banks financed "terrorism".

Prince Mohammad al-Faisal al-Saud, chairman of Geneva-based Dar al-Mal al-Islami (Islamic Money House) and the International Association of Islamic Banks, said: "Let those who accuse us of financing terrorism produce the evidence -- if there is any -- of what they claim."
The prince, son of the late King Faisal who was assassinated by a nephew in 1975, did not say who had made the allegations.

But he told the daily Gulf News: "How can Islamic banks, which are entrusted with people's money, give themselves the right to finance activities which have not been authorised by the financiers? Moreover, what is to be got out of financing terrorism when we must provide profits for those who deposit their money with us."

Prince Mohammed, speaking on the sidelines of the annual Islamic Banking and Finance Forum in Dubai, said he was unaware of claims that Islamic charitable societies misused cash they collected in zakat al-fitr, money paid by every Moslem at the end of the fasting month Ramadan, and zakat al-mal, an annual levy on a Moslem's wealth, to finance terrorist groups.

"I do not know about others. But what I can say about Dar al-Mal al-Islami is that we have zakat funds which we manage ourselves and we know how and where the money is spent. All our activities are clear to central banks who have full, detailed financial reports on our budgets."

Gulf officials had said earlier this year that the United States urged some of the Gulf Arab states to check Moslem charities for fears funds were filtering through to militant Palestinian groups blamed for a wave of bombings in Israel.

Speaking about Islamic "terrorist" movements, the prince said: "I reject the use of the term 'Islamic movements' as we are all Moslems. In fact, there are assassinations and explosions all over the place which have nothing to do with the spirit of Islam."

Two bombs in Saudi Arabia over the last year have killed 24 American servicemen and two Indians. Four Saudis subsequently executed for their role in the first blast said in televised confessions they were influenced by Saudi dissidents abroad.
U.S. officials have named Osama bin Laden, a financier stripped of his Saudi citizenship, as a prime suspect in the bombings.
